title: Quantum simulation of neutrino oscillations with bosonic encoding
abstract: Superconducting qubits offer a versatile platform for quantum simulation. In this architecture, quantum information can be encoded in the bosonic modes of a microwave cavity, offering an alternative to conventional qubit-based encoding schemes. These cavity bosonic modes can be manipulated using a single ancillary qubit. In this work, we investigate the quantum simulation of two- and three-flavor neutrino oscillations using Fock-basis encoding of a cavity mode. We design pulse sequences for implementing the required unitary operations through selective number-dependent arbitrary phase (SNAP) and displacement gates. Pulse-level control is employed to realize high-fidelity gate operations on the encoded cavity mode. The resulting neutrino oscillation probabilities obtained from quantum simulation exhibit close agreement with the corresponding theoretical predictions, demonstrating the feasibility of cavity-based bosonic encoding schemes for quantum simulation.
summary: The paper details the use of superconducting microwave cavities with bosonic encoding to simulate fundamental particle physics processes, specifically neutrino oscillations. By synthesizing arbitrary unitary gates using Displacement and SNAP operations, the authors demonstrate that this cavity platform can accurately model these complex quantum dynamics. This establishes a strong link between advanced quantum control in circuit QED and high-energy physics simulation.
main_problem: The primary goal is the quantum simulation of two- and three-flavor neutrino oscillations using superconducting circuits.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that cavity-based bosonic encoding provides a viable platform for this simulation, showing agreement between simulated probabilities and theoretical predictions.
method: They implement required unitary operations by combining Displacement gates and Selective Number-dependent Arbitrary Phase (SNAP) gates through carefully designed pulse sequences.
model_or_system: The system uses superconducting qubits coupled to a microwave cavity mode. Information is encoded in the bosonic Fock states of the cavity ($\{|nangle\}$), allowing for qudit representation, which is controlled via dispersive coupling and ancillary qubit manipulation.

paper_structure: The paper first details the universal control scheme using bosonic encoding (D and S gates). It then applies this framework to compile the necessary unitaries for simulating neutrino oscillations in both two- and three-flavor scenarios, comparing direct compilation vs. pulse-level simulation results.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Universal control of a cavity bosonic mode using displacement and SNAP gates. An arbitrary unitary operation in a d-dimensional cavity subspace can be decomposed into a sequence of k + 1 displacement gates, D(α), and k SNAP gates, S (⃗θ). In this work, displacement operations are implemented using short Gaussian-shaped control pulses applied through cavity drive, while SNAP gates are realized using longer flat-top Gaussian pulses that induce photon-number- dependent rotations of the ancilla qubit. Together, these operations provide universal control over the cavity Hilbert space.

Figure 2: Quantum simulation of two-flavor neutrino vacuum oscillation for the Fock-state-encoded cavity qubits. The solid line represents the theoretical prediction (θvac = 33.5◦, ∆m2 = 7.5×10−5 eV2), while the symbols correspond to the quantum simulation results obtained using direct compilation [Eq. (21)] and pulse-level simulation [Appendix A].

Figure 3: Wigner function of the neutrino flavor state |νµ⟩, initially encoded in the cavity Fock state |1⟩. As the neutrino propagates, flavor mixing causes the encoded cavity state to evolve. The top row shows the theoretically predicted states, while the bottom row shows the corresponding pulse-level simulation results.

Figure 4: Pulse-level simulation of three-flavor neutrino oscillations. The three flavor states are encoded in the cavity Fock subspace {|0⟩, |1⟩, |2⟩}. The neutrino mixing matrix is compiled using two building blocks of the form (B.1) and the parameters of the SNAP and displacement gates are optimized numerically using the qgrad package.
